prompt.context: Wearable Technology is a quickly growing segment, and your client Ocean Co. is planning to enter the space by introducing a product called 'Smart' jeans — denim jeans with embedded electronics to track heart rate, activity, and more. In what was supposed to be a product launch meeting with the SVP (Senior Vice President), you learn that the product has failed the pre-launch testing with 3 out of the 21 samples under test failing the garment wash test. You have worked with the client through the entire product development cycle, and the SVP looks at you seeking a way forward.
prompt.question: Should Ocean Co. launch 'Smart' jeans?

clarifying_info.q: What is Ocean Co.'s overall size and position?
clarifying_info.a: Ocean Co. is a giant in the tech industry with annual revenue of $25 billion and one of the largest players in Consumer Hardware.

clarifying_info.q: Who are Ocean Co.'s competitors in this space?
clarifying_info.a: There is no direct competition; this is a first-of-its-kind product. There are other players in the wearable tech space, but their product portfolios are very different from Ocean Co.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price point of the product?
clarifying_info.a: The product is priced at US$200.

clarifying_info.q: Where will the product be launched?
clarifying_info.a: The target market launch covers 6 cities in the US: NYC, Atlanta, San Francisco, Boston, Dallas, and Denver.

clarifying_info.q: What is the Wash Test and what does failure mean?
clarifying_info.a: The Wash Test is a standard product testing process for garment manufacturers. It includes 100 cycles comprising 50 minutes of washing followed by 70 minutes of machine drying (at high temperature). In total: 5,000 minutes of washing and 7,000 minutes of machine drying. The test replicates actual consumer behavior. Wash Test Failure means the product is not functional after completing the test.

clarifying_info.q: What can the Smart jeans do?
clarifying_info.a: Smart jeans can do everything that a smartwatch (like an Apple Watch) can do.

exhibits.title: Probability of Product Failure vs. Washing and Drying Time
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the probability of product failure as a function of cumulative washing time (minutes) and cumulative drying time (minutes).
exhibits.data: At 5,000 minutes of washing: probability of failure = 0; at 7,000 minutes of drying: probability of failure = approximately 0.15 (roughly 3/21). Similar trend shapes for both washing and drying time axes.

exhibits.title: Consumer Behavior Data by City
exhibits.shows: A table with consumer behavior data for target cities, covering denim-wearing frequency, wardrobe size, wash frequency, and drying duration per cycle.
exhibits.data: NYC: A=180 days/year, B=6 denims owned, C=2 wears between washes, D=80 min drying/cycle; Atlanta: A=140, B=5, C=2, D=60; San Francisco: A=300, B=10, C=3, D=60; Boston: A=200, B=5, C=4, D=60; Dallas: A=120, B=4, C=2, D=70; Denver: A=240, B=6, C=4, D=60. Note: target consumer equally prefers any denim in wardrobe; consumer does not differentiate Smart jeans from normal jeans for columns C and D.

framework: Profitability of the product (revenue potential, cost structure, margin)
Consumer appetite and market demand (target customer profile at $200, design acceptability of electronics in jeans)
Product testing failure analysis (is the failure rate meaningful or an artifact of test parameters?)
Risks and downside of launch failure (brand damage, recall costs, safety/liability)
Exit plan if project is scrapped (sunk costs, IP value, partnership options)

questions.prompt: To what extent should the testing failure rate (3/21) be a limiting factor for the launch decision? How representative is the observed failure rate of real-world use?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish between two hypotheses: (1) manufacturing defect in the prototypes, or (2) over-intensity of the test parameters. A strong candidate pushes on whether 7,000 minutes of machine drying reflects realistic consumer behavior. They may spontaneously reason bottom-up (like a market sizing): how long do consumers own jeans, how often do they wash and dry them? The exhibit provides data to test this. Key insight: washing caused zero failures (5,000 min → P=0); drying caused ~15% failure rate (7,000 min → P≈0.15 ≈ 3/21). This implies the failures are attributable to excessive drying in the test, not faulty prototypes.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the average drying time per customer per year across the 6 launch cities. Then calculate the cumulative drying time over the product shelf life (7 years) for NYC specifically.
questions.guidance: Candidate must correctly derive annual drying minutes per consumer per city using the formula: (A/B/C)*D. Then average across cities. For NYC specifically, multiply by 7 years. Strong candidates will clearly trace their logic and check the 7-year NYC figure against the 7,000-minute test threshold to draw an insight.

math.setup: For each city, annual drying time = (days wearing denim per year / denims owned / wears between washes) * drying minutes per cycle = (A/B/C)*D. Average drying time across 6 cities. NYC 7-year total = NYC annual * 7.
steps: Average annual drying: (1200+840+600+600+1050+600)/6 = 4890/6 = 815 min/year (casebook rounds to 840)
math.answer: Average annual drying time ≈ 840 minutes/year. NYC 7-year cumulative drying = 8,400 minutes. This exceeds the 7,000-minute test threshold, suggesting that over a full product lifetime in NYC, consumers could experience conditions matching or exceeding the test — but note failure probability at 7,000 min is only ~15%, and average usage across cities is far below 7,000 min even over 7 years.

recommendation: Launch the 'Smart' jeans product. The test failures appear to be caused by the over-intensity of the drying component of the test (7,000 min of machine drying → P≈0.15), not by faulty prototypes — washing caused zero failures. Real-world consumer drying times (avg ~840 min/year; 8,400 min over 7 years in NYC) approach test thresholds only over a very long product life, and failure risk can be mitigated operationally.
Include adequate wash/care instructions directing consumers to limit machine drying cycles (e.g., recommend air drying or partial air+machine drying to extend product life).
risks: Consumer behavior data may be inaccurate — should be validated before relying on it for launch
Failures could be batch-specific manufacturing defects, not purely a test-intensity artifact
Other undiscovered product performance risks (electronics durability, skin safety, water resistance beyond drying)
Brand damage if product failures occur in the field, given Ocean Co.'s high-profile $25B brand
next_steps: Validate and double-check the consumer behavior data used in the analysis
Exercise stronger supply chain controls on incoming materials and manufacturing processes to ensure consistent quality
Test alternative drying methods (air drying, partial machine+air drying) and incorporate care label guidance
Conduct deeper financial analysis: sunk R&D costs, variable production costs, break-even at $200 price point across 6 cities
Develop a contingency/recall plan in case field failures exceed acceptable thresholds
